text: Kesh sent you. She said you'd played one game, and that you were frightened for most of it.
That's normal. Let me set you a position. Black to play, and exactly one move matters.
The board will keep.
The position is still on the small board. Black to play.
Good. Count the liberties before you decide anything else. That was your first lesson, and it was short.
This is the Essenveld Instituut. Marguerite, at the desk in the hall, keeps the register. Tell her I sent you.
They take beginners. You play in the league, and you come here for the classes.
The demonstration board at the front is where I teach. Use it when you like.
You're going to ask me for a game. Not yet. Finish the course first. Then it's worth the afternoon.
You've had the course. A teaching game, then. You take Black, and as many stones as the gap says.

exit.intro: A teaching game. She sets the bowls down and waits.

text: When you walked in here you did not know what a liberty was.
An even game, then. I will not go easy, and you will lose. Watch what it costs me.

exit.intro: Even. She has not offered anyone this in some time.
A teaching game. She sets the bowls down and waits.

text: Of course.
Ah. I'm going to sit with that for a moment.
Then I'm going to ask you what you thought I was doing on move nine.
Before I say anything: what was the last move you were sure about?
Not the last good one. The last one you were sure of. The game was after it.
Good. Say it back to yourself, silently. That's the shape of every class here.
Three numbers: your liberties, theirs, and whose move it is. You'll forget for a year. Then you won't.
Before you call something an eye, look at the stones making it and ask whether they are one group.
I heard. You're the same strength today as you were yesterday. The card did nothing. The games did.
Nineteen lines next, and you know almost nothing about it. Isn't that good?
I heard. Sit down, you're allowed.
I failed that exam twice. Three games decided it, and you can name what went wrong in each. That's a lot.
